idiom_name: Task and async-await for the async layer, AsyncStream as the queueing layer
implementation_notes: Structured concurrency is the asynchronous layer: a Task runs a unit of asynchronous work on the cooperative pool while I/O suspends instead of blocking, and an AsyncStream or an actor's mailbox is the queueing layer handing work to the synchronous layer. Blocking service code is moved to a dedicated DispatchQueue (or a detached Task that calls the blocking API), which plays the part of the worker pool; the classic form is still justified when the blocking code is an unchangeable C or Objective-C library. Because tasks are not threads, the layering only holds if no blocking call is made from an async function.
pitfalls: Blocking the cooperative pool - a synchronous file read, a semaphore wait - starves other tasks; offload to DispatchQueue.async or a detached Task.
AsyncStream continuations have no built-in bound and are single-consumer by default, so work can be accepted faster than the worker side drains it.
Cancelling the consuming task does not propagate into the DispatchQueue worker; the synchronous layer must check cancellation itself.

variants.name: DispatchQueue event sources with a serial worker queue (pre-async)
variants.idiom_name: DispatchSource/readability handlers plus an OperationQueue with a semaphore gate
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-async design used on older deployment targets: a DispatchSource or run-loop readability handler is the asynchronous layer, a DispatchSemaphore bounds the queue, and an OperationQueue (or a fixed set of serial queues) with limited concurrency is the synchronous layer. Choose it when the code must interoperate with completion-handler APIs or support OS versions without Swift concurrency; the queue bound, worker count and shutdown ordering are all your responsibility.
pitfalls: Waiting on the semaphore from the main queue deadlocks the UI; only wait inside the event source's queue or a background queue.
A DispatchSource handler that performs the blocking work itself turns the event queue into the bottleneck.
OperationQueue has no back-pressure of its own: without the semaphore gate the pending-operation set grows unbounded.
